title: A training-only false-signal gate beat the response-class rule in five new climate-response families (11,791 series, 2005-2024); a trend-preserving null corrected its one wrong choice
abstract: Question: can training years alone, without a response-class label, show whether climate terms will add forecast skill in a new family of climate-response relations, and does a null that keeps shared trends remove the false signals that a shifted-climate null misses? Approach: we froze a timestamped plan with the exploratory family gate of sci:sha256:8804b69f (frozen climate slope with a 5-year trailing level if the family false-signal rate FSR <= 0.32, else the trailing mean), a new trend-preserving null (each climate predictor keeps its linear training trend; only residuals are shifted) and six decision rules. We applied them unchanged to five new families (11,791 series; training to 2004, test 2005-2024): German wild-plant phases to June and after June, German field-crop phases, English river invertebrate abundance and national crop yields. Results: the FSR gate beat the response-class rule (pooled skill +0.023, 95% interval 0.018 to 0.029); they disagreed in one family (late plant phases, timing class), where the gate was right. FSR ordered forward skill again (rho -0.90 in new families, -0.88 over 18 units, p = 0.0001). The trend-preserving null raised FSR most for crop yields (0.48 to 1.00), kept spring phenology low (0.23), chose the best fixed strategy in all five families, corrected the gate's error in field crops (+0.011) and lowered series losses (crop yields 26% to 0%). The trailing mean beat the training mean in all five families. Two predictions failed: the frozen FSR equation did not predict outcome size better than class means, and within-family screening did not follow the gate (3 of 5). Exploratory: rebuilt earlier families reproduced their FSR exactly; the trend null cut dengue losses from 21% to 1.4%. Limitations: one disagreeing family; the trend null was designed after the dengue failure; single-window linear models with observed weather.
